lessonTitle: Point and Line Defects in Crystals

blocks.text: A pure copper single crystal can be bent by hand like a soft wire, yet its atomic bonds are strong enough that a perfect crystal of copper would need billions of pascals of shear stress to deform. Imperfections in the lattice explain the gap, and they also let atoms move during heat treatment.

blocks.markdown: A real crystal is never perfect. **Point defects** involve one or a few atomic sites: a *vacancy* is an empty lattice site, a *self-interstitial* is a host atom squeezed into a void, a *substitutional* solute atom replaces a host atom, and an *interstitial* solute atom (such as carbon in iron) sits in a void between host atoms. **Line defects** (dislocations) are one-dimensional: they are the boundary between slipped and unslipped regions of a crystal.

blocks.title: Equilibrium vacancy fraction
blocks.text: The fraction of lattice sites that are vacant at thermal equilibrium: $N_v/N=\exp(-Q_v/kT)$, where $Q_v$ is the energy to form one vacancy (eV per vacancy), $k=8.62\times10^{-5}$ eV/K is Boltzmann's constant and $T$ is absolute temperature in kelvin. If $Q_v$ is expressed per mole (J/mol), replace $k$ with the gas constant $R=8.314$ J/(mol K).

blocks.caption: Arrhenius form: vacancies cost energy $Q_v$ but increase entropy, so some always exist above 0 K.

blocks.title: Vacancies in aluminium at high and low temperature
blocks.prompt: Aluminium has $Q_v\approx0.75$ eV (typical). Compare the vacancy fraction at 900 K (near its melting point of 933 K) with that at 300 K.
blocks.answer: About 6 vacancies in $10^5$ sites near the melting point against 2.5 in $10^{13}$ at room temperature: a factor of about $10^8$, which is why diffusion by vacancy jumps is so strongly temperature dependent.

blocks.markdown: **Burgers vector.** Draw a closed loop atom by atom in a perfect crystal. Draw the same sequence of steps around a dislocation and the loop fails to close. The closure failure is the **Burgers vector** $\mathbf b$, a lattice translation vector whose magnitude is one interatomic distance along the slip direction. For FCC metals $|\mathbf b|=a/\sqrt2$ (that is, $\tfrac a2\langle110\rangle$); for BCC metals $|\mathbf b|=\sqrt3\,a/2$ (that is, $\tfrac a2\langle111\rangle$).

rows: Extra half-plane of atoms ending at the line
Planes spiral around the line like a helical ramp
blocks.caption: Mixed dislocations have a line direction between the two and are made of edge and screw components.

blocks.markdown: **Why metals are weaker than theory.** To shear one plane of a perfect crystal rigidly over another every bond across the plane must stretch at once. A simple model gives a theoretical shear strength of about $\tau_{th}\approx G/(2\pi)$, where $G$ is the shear modulus. Real metals have yield shear stresses 100 to 10000 times smaller. They deform because dislocations glide: at any instant only the row of atoms next to the dislocation line changes its neighbours, so only a small force is needed, rather like moving a ripple along a carpet instead of dragging the whole carpet.

blocks.title: Theoretical shear strength against observation
blocks.prompt: Aluminium has $G\approx26$ GPa. Estimate $\tau_{th}$ and compare it with an observed single-crystal yield shear stress of about 1 MPa (typical order).

steps.text: Form the ratio of theory to observation.

blocks.answer: $\tau_{th}\approx4$ GPa, about 4000 times the observed stress. The gap is explained by dislocation glide.

items: Vacancies and interstitials control diffusion; their number rises exponentially with temperature.
Dislocations control plastic deformation; their motion makes metals ductile and weak compared with theory.
Anything that obstructs dislocation motion (solute atoms, other dislocations, grain boundaries, precipitates) raises strength.
Interstitial solutes (C, N, H) distort the lattice more than substitutional solutes of similar size.

blocks.title: Two exponentials to remember
blocks.text: Vacancy fraction grows as $\exp(-Q_v/kT)$ and diffusion as $\exp(-Q_d/RT)$. In both, small increases in temperature near the melting point change the numbers by orders of magnitude.

points: Point defects are vacancies, self-interstitials, and substitutional or interstitial solutes; equilibrium vacancy fraction is $N_v/N=\exp(-Q_v/kT)$.
The Burgers vector is the lattice closure failure: perpendicular to the line for an edge dislocation and parallel for a screw.
Real metals yield far below the theoretical shear strength $G/(2\pi)$ because dislocations glide, shifting one row of bonds at a time.

questions.stem: An edge dislocation in a crystal is characterised by which geometric relation between its Burgers vector $\mathbf b$ and its dislocation line direction $\mathbf t$?

options.text: $\mathbf b$ makes no fixed angle to $\mathbf t$ in any dislocation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the extra half-plane edge defines the line, and the lattice displacement $\mathbf b$ lies in the plane perpendicular to it.
distractorRationale.b: This is the definition of a screw dislocation.
distractorRationale.c: The Burgers vector of any dislocation is non-zero; it is the closure failure of a Burgers circuit.
distractorRationale.d: Pure edge and pure screw dislocations have fixed angles (90 and 0 degrees); only mixed dislocations have intermediate angles.

questions.explanation: A Burgers circuit around an edge dislocation fails to close by a vector perpendicular to the dislocation line, because the extra half-plane terminates at the line. For a screw dislocation the closure failure is parallel to the line, and for mixed dislocations the angle lies between the two.

questions.stem: In a plain-carbon steel, carbon atoms sit in the spaces between iron atoms, whereas in a brass alloy zinc atoms replace copper atoms on lattice sites. How are these point defects classified?

options.text: Carbon is interstitial and zinc is substitutional
Carbon is substitutional and zinc is interstitial

questions.correctOptionText: Carbon is interstitial and zinc is substitutional

distractorRationale.a: Correct: small atoms that fit in the voids are interstitials; atoms of similar size that take lattice sites are substitutional.
distractorRationale.b: A vacancy is an empty lattice site, not a foreign atom.
distractorRationale.c: The roles are reversed; carbon is too small to replace an iron atom and sits in a void.
distractorRationale.d: A self-interstitial is a host atom squeezed into a void, not a foreign atom.

questions.explanation: Point defects involve single atomic sites: vacancies (empty sites), self-interstitials, substitutional solute atoms on lattice sites and interstitial solute atoms in voids. Carbon in iron is the standard interstitial solute because its radius is far smaller than that of iron.

questions.stem: A perfect crystal with no vacancies is the equilibrium state of a metal at any temperature above absolute zero.
questions.explanation: Vacancies raise the internal energy but also increase entropy, and at any temperature above 0 K the free energy is minimised with a finite equilibrium fraction of vacancies. The fraction is $\exp(-Q_v/kT)$, which rises steeply with temperature.

questions.stem: Silver has a vacancy formation energy of about $Q_v=1.1$ eV per vacancy (typical value). Using Boltzmann's constant $k=8.62\times10^{-5}$ eV/K, calculate the equilibrium vacancy fraction $N_v/N$ at 1000 K, in units of $10^{-6}$.
questions.explanation: The equilibrium fraction is $N_v/N=\exp(-Q_v/kT)$. The exponent is $-1.1/(8.62\times10^{-5}\times1000)=-12.76$, so $N_v/N=e^{-12.76}=2.87\times10^{-6}$, about 3 vacancies per million lattice sites.

questions.stem: A metal has a vacancy formation energy of 0.90 eV. At what absolute temperature in K does the equilibrium vacancy fraction reach $1.0\times10^{-4}$? Use $k=8.62\times10^{-5}$ eV/K.
The theoretical shear strength of a perfect crystal can be estimated as $\tau_{th}\approx G/(2\pi)$. For a steel with shear modulus $G=80$ GPa, calculate $\tau_{th}$ in GPa.
questions.explanation: Using $\tau_{th}\approx G/(2\pi)=80/6.283=12.7$ GPa. This is far above the shear stresses at which real steels yield (of the order of tens to hundreds of MPa), which is the discrepancy explained by dislocations.

questions.stem: A dislocation line lies along $[1\bar{1}0]$ in a crystal and its Burgers vector is $\mathbf b=\tfrac{a}{2}[1\bar{1}0]$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a pure screw dislocation, since $\mathbf b$ is parallel to the line; under shear the line moves perpendicular to $\mathbf b$
It is a pure edge dislocation, since $\mathbf b$ is parallel to the line
It is a pure edge dislocation that moves parallel to $\mathbf b$
It is a vacancy cluster, because $\mathbf b$ has length $a/\sqrt2$

questions.correctOptionText: It is a pure screw dislocation, since $\mathbf b$ is parallel to the line; under shear the line moves perpendicular to $\mathbf b$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: parallel $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf t$ is a screw, and its line sweeps sideways across the slip plane.
distractorRationale.b: An edge dislocation has $\mathbf b$ perpendicular to the line.
distractorRationale.c: Edge dislocations do move parallel to $\mathbf b$, but this one has $\mathbf b$ parallel to the line, so it is not an edge.
distractorRationale.d: Burgers vectors are lattice translation vectors; a vacancy cluster has no Burgers vector in this sense.

questions.explanation: Because $\mathbf b$ is parallel to the line direction, the dislocation is pure screw. A screw dislocation moves in a direction perpendicular to its Burgers vector (and line), while the crystal above and below the slip plane is displaced by $\mathbf b$, the same total slip as for an edge.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for real metals yielding at shear stresses roughly $10^{3}$ to $10^{4}$ times smaller than $G/(2\pi)$?

options.text: Slip occurs by the movement of dislocations, which shifts one row of bonds at a time instead of shearing a whole plane at once
Real metals contain more bonds per unit area than the perfect-crystal model
The perfect-crystal model uses the wrong value of Young's modulus
Real metals are amorphous, so slip planes do not exist

questions.correctOptionText: Slip occurs by the movement of dislocations, which shifts one row of bonds at a time instead of shearing a whole plane at once

distractorRationale.a: Correct: only a line of atoms is displaced at each moment, so far less force is needed.
distractorRationale.b: The bond density is the same; the difference is the mechanism of slip.
distractorRationale.c: The model gives the stress to shear whole planes rigidly past each other, which is correctly of order $G/(2\pi)$ for a perfect lattice.
distractorRationale.d: Metals are crystalline; slip planes exist, and dislocations glide on them.

questions.explanation: The theoretical estimate assumes every bond across a plane is stretched together. A moving dislocation shifts the crystal one row of atoms at a time, like moving a ripple through a carpet, and the required stress is orders of magnitude lower.

questions.stem: Distinguish edge and screw dislocations. Describe a Burgers circuit and state, for each type, the relation between the Burgers vector and the line direction and the direction in which the dislocation moves under an applied shear stress.
markingGuide: Burgers circuit: a closed atom-to-atom loop in the perfect lattice that fails to close around a dislocation; the closure vector is $\mathbf b$ (2 marks)
Edge: extra half-plane of atoms, $\mathbf b$ perpendicular to the line (1 mark)
Screw: helical ramp of planes, $\mathbf b$ parallel to the line (1 mark)
Edge dislocation moves parallel to $\mathbf b$ in the slip plane (1 mark)
Screw dislocation moves perpendicular to $\mathbf b$ (and to its line) (1 mark)
Both produce the same slip displacement $\mathbf b$ across the slip plane (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The Burgers circuit gives the magnitude and direction of lattice distortion. Edge has $\mathbf b\perp$ line and glides along $\mathbf b$; screw has $\mathbf b\parallel$ line and glides perpendicular to $\mathbf b$, but both shear the crystal by $\mathbf b$.

questions.stem: Pure aluminium single crystals yield at a shear stress of only about 1 MPa (typical order), whereas $G/(2\pi)$ for aluminium with $G\approx26$ GPa is about 4 GPa. Explain the discrepancy and explain why the yield strength of a real alloy can be raised well above that of the pure metal.
markingGuide: $G/(2\pi)\approx4.1$ GPa, thousands of times larger than the observed stress (1 mark)
The estimate assumes simultaneous shearing of an entire plane of atoms (1 mark)
Real crystals contain dislocations that glide at a low stress because only a line of bonds is broken at a time (2 marks)
Yield strength is therefore set by the stress to move dislocations (1 mark)
Alloying, cold work and grain refinement raise the stress by obstructing dislocation motion (solute atoms, other dislocations, grain boundaries) (2 marks)
Whiskers or defect-free crystals approach the theoretical value because they lack mobile dislocations (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The theoretical strength is about $G/(2\pi)\approx4$ GPa, but dislocation glide allows yielding at about 1 MPa for pure aluminium. Barriers to dislocation motion raise this stress, which is why alloys and cold-worked metals are stronger.
